samples.text:
In many countries, young people are moving from villages to cities to study or to find better jobs, and only old people stay in the countryside. This situation causes several problems for rural communities, and in this essay I will discuss them and suggest some solutions.

The first problem is the economy. When young people leave, there are not enough workers for farms and local business, so many of them have to close. For example, a village shop or a small factory cannot continue if there is no customers or employees. Another problem is that the elderly people need more care, but there is nobody to look after them. Their children live far away in the city, and often there are not enough doctors and nurses in rural area. Also, services like schools, banks and bus routes are closed because there are not enough people to use them, and this make life even more difficult for the ones who stay.

There are some solutions for these problems. Firstly, the government should create more jobs in the countryside, for example by giving money to companies which open offices or factories there. Secondly, it is important to have fast internet in the villages, because then young people can work online from home and they do not need to move away. In addition, the government can improve health services for old people, like mobile clinics which visit different villages every week.

In conclusion, when young people move to cities, rural areas suffer from economic problems and poor care for the elderly. I believe that with more jobs, better internet and better services, the countryside can become a good place for young people again.
samples.why: Both parts addressed with relevant problems and solutions · explanation is limited and conclusion rather general · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, article and plural errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
In many parts of the world, rural areas are experiencing a steady outflow of young people who move to cities in search of education, jobs and a more exciting lifestyle. As a result, many villages are left with an ageing population, which creates serious difficulties. This essay will outline these problems and suggest some possible solutions.

The most immediate problem is economic decline. When young adults leave, local farms and businesses lose both workers and customers, and many are eventually forced to close. This in turn makes the area even less attractive to newcomers, creating a cycle of decline. A second problem concerns the care of the elderly. Older residents often need more medical support, yet rural areas typically has fewer doctors and hospitals, and the relatives who might once have cared for them now live far away. Finally, as the population falls, services such as schools, post offices and public transport become harder to justify financially and are often withdrawn, leaving remaining residents increasingly isolated.

Tackling these issues requires making rural areas places where young people can build a future. Investment in high-speed broadband is particularly important, since it would allow people to work remotely for city-based employers while living in the countryside. Governments could also offer incentives, such as tax reductions or grants, to businesses that set up in rural regions, and support young farmers with loans and training. At the same time, services for the elderly must be adapted to rural conditions. Mobile health clinics, online consultations and community transport schemes could ensure that older residents receive care without long journeys. Encouraging volunteer networks within villages would also help to reduce isolation.

In conclusion, the migration of young people to cities leaves rural communities facing economic decline, pressure on elderly care and the loss of services. Better connectivity, economic incentives and adapted services could help to reverse this trend.
samples.why: Clear position · three problems extended, including a cycle of decline · solutions address both young people and elderly residents · good cohesion and vocabulary (outflow, connectivity) · one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Across many countries, the countryside is emptying of its young. Drawn by universities, better-paid work and the amenities of urban life, school leavers and young adults depart in large numbers, and relatively few return. The communities they leave behind grow steadily older, facing a combination of economic, social and practical difficulties that call for deliberate intervention.

The economic consequences are often the first to appear. Farms struggle to find successors and seasonal labour, while shops and small firms lose both staff and customers. Each closure makes the area less appealing to potential residents, so decline tends to become self-reinforcing. Demographic ageing then compounds the problem. Older residents typically require more health and social care, yet rural areas are already poorly served by doctors and hospitals, and the adult children who might once have provided informal support now live hours away. As numbers fall further, schools, bank branches and bus routes are withdrawn on grounds of cost, leaving those who remain, particularly people who no longer drive, isolated and dependent.

Reversing this trend requires giving young people genuine reasons to stay or return. The most powerful lever is probably digital infrastructure: reliable high-speed broadband makes remote work viable, allowing professionals to hold city-based jobs while living rurally. Targeted incentives, such as grants for rural start-ups, affordable housing reserved for local families and support for young farmers, can reinforce this. Services, meanwhile, must be redesigned rather than simply withdrawn. Remote consultations, visiting clinics and shared community hubs that combine a post office, café and health point can maintain access at a sustainable cost. Intergenerational initiatives, such as young volunteers assisting older neighbours, can also strengthen the social fabric.

In conclusion, the exodus of young people leaves rural communities economically fragile, short of care and increasingly isolated. With investment in connectivity, targeted incentives and imaginative service provision, the countryside can once again offer a viable future to the young.
samples.why: Both parts sufficiently addressed with well-developed, interconnected ideas · solutions clearly matched to problems · skilful cohesion · precise vocabulary (self-reinforcing, exodus, social fabric) · wide range of accurate structures.
